seo_title: Hip Replacement Rehab in North Palm Beach | First Rehab
seo_desc: Physical therapy after hip replacement in North Palm Beach. One-on-one rehab that follows your surgeon's precautions and rebuilds walking. Medicare accepted.
lede: Physical therapy after hip replacement that respects your surgeon's precautions while you rebuild hip strength, balance and a steady walk.
what_it_is: In a total hip replacement, the surgeon removes the damaged ball at the top of the thighbone and replaces it with a metal stem topped by a metal or ceramic ball. The worn socket in the pelvis is lined with a metal shell and a plastic, ceramic or metal liner. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, citing federal data, reports that more than 450,000 of these surgeries are done each year in the United States.

According to the AAOS, most people who have a hip replacement are between 50 and 80. The new joint addresses the painful surfaces, but the hip muscles that were weakened by years of arthritis and by the surgery itself need retraining. Rehab helps you walk without a limp, protect the new joint while it settles in, and return to the low impact activities you enjoy, all within the protocol your surgeon sets.
symptoms: Weak hip muscles, especially on the side of the buttock
Limping or leaning to one side when walking
Stiffness in the hip and thigh
Swelling in the thigh, knee or ankle
Reliance on a walker, crutches or cane
Trouble with stairs, low chairs, and getting in and out of a car
Unsteady balance and worry about the new hip slipping
causes: Osteoarthritis, the most common reason for hip replacement
Rheumatoid arthritis and related inflammatory joint diseases
Posttraumatic arthritis after a hip injury or fracture
Osteonecrosis, when poor blood supply causes the femoral head to collapse
Childhood hip disease that leads to arthritis later in life
Hip pain and stiffness that limit daily activities or persist at rest despite medicines and therapy

how_therapy_helps.intro: The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons describes exercise as a key part of recovery at home, including a graduated walking program and specific exercises done several times a day to restore movement and strength. A 2022 systematic review in the American Journal of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation found low-strength evidence that different rehabilitation programs after hip replacement may give similar results for pain, strength and daily activities. In practice, following the protocol your surgeon prescribes, done consistently and progressed safely, is a sound approach.
methods: Progressive exercises for the muscles that hold your pelvis level when you stand on one leg, which helps reduce limping.
Practice walking with your walker, crutches or cane, then stepping down to less support when your surgeon and therapist agree it is safe.
Learning to sit, stand, dress, bathe and get in and out of bed or a car while following the hip precautions your surgeon assigns.
Standing and stepping drills that build confidence and lower the chance of a fall, which can damage a new hip.
A walking plan that starts indoors and progresses outside as your endurance improves, as the AAOS recommends.
Exercises you repeat several times a day between visits, updated as you get stronger.

first_visit: Your first visit lasts about an hour and includes treatment the same day. Your therapist reviews your surgeon's protocol, your weight bearing status and any hip precautions you were given. They check hip motion within your allowed limits, test strength in the hip and thigh, and watch how you walk, turn, sit and stand. They also look at balance and how you manage stairs. You leave with a home program that fits your precautions.
recovery: Every recovery is different, and your surgeon sets the timeline. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons says most people can resume light daily activities within 3 to 6 weeks after a hip replacement. MedlinePlus notes that most people no longer need a walker or crutches after 2 to 4 weeks and that you should have someone with you at home for the first 1 to 2 weeks. MedlinePlus also advises extra care to avoid dislocating the new hip, especially in the first few months. Health, strength before surgery and the surgical approach all affect pace.
self_care: Follow every hip precaution your surgeon gave you, since rules can differ by surgical approach.
Avoid low chairs and soft sofas, and use a firm chair with arms, as MedlinePlus advises.
Get up and walk at least every 45 minutes instead of sitting for long periods.
Use your walker or crutches until your surgeon says you can stop.
Keep walkways clear of rugs and cords, and carry small items in a bag on your walker so your hands stay free.
see_a_doctor: Your hip feels like it slipped out of place, or you suddenly cannot move or bear weight on the leg
Pain or swelling in your calf or leg, especially if the leg is red and warmer than the other, which can signal a blood clot
Sudden shortness of breath or chest pain (call 911)
Fever above 101°F, chills, or redness, drainage or increasing pain at the incision
A fall or injury to the leg that had surgery
A sudden increase in hip pain or pain your medicine does not control

faqs.q: What are hip precautions after hip replacement?
faqs.a: Hip precautions are movement rules that lower the risk of dislocating a new hip. MedlinePlus lists common ones: do not cross your legs, avoid bending the hip past 90 degrees, do not bend far forward at the waist, and do not sleep on your stomach or the operated side. Surgeons assign precautions based on how the surgery was done, so follow your own surgeon's list.

faqs.q: How long will I need a walker after hip replacement?
faqs.a: MedlinePlus says most people stop using a walker or crutches 2 to 4 weeks after hip replacement surgery. The exact timing depends on your weight bearing instructions, strength and balance. Check with your surgeon before you stop using your walking aid. Your physical therapist can help you move from a walker to a cane and then to walking on your own.

faqs.q: Why do I still limp after my hip replacement?
faqs.a: A limp after hip replacement often comes from weak hip muscles, especially those on the side of the buttock that keep your pelvis level as you step. Pain, stiffness and habits formed before surgery can add to it. Strengthening and gait training in physical therapy target these causes. Tell your surgeon about a limp that is getting worse rather than better.

faqs.q: Does it matter which rehab program I do after hip replacement?
faqs.a: A 2022 systematic review in the American Journal of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation compared different rehabilitation programs after hip replacement and found they did not differ much for pain, strength, daily activities or quality of life. The authors rated the evidence as low and called for more research. Following your surgeon's protocol consistently is the practical takeaway.

faqs.q: What activities can I do after a hip replacement?
faqs.a: According to MedlinePlus, most people can eventually return to low impact activities such as hiking, gardening, swimming, tennis and golf. Downhill skiing and contact sports such as football and soccer are usually off the list. Your surgeon decides when you are cleared for each activity, and your therapist can help you build the strength to get there.

faqs.q: How common are complications after hip replacement?
faqs.a: The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons reports that serious complications such as joint infection occur in fewer than 2 percent of hip replacement patients. Blood clots and dislocation are other known risks. Knowing the warning signs, such as calf swelling, fever, or a feeling that the hip has slipped, helps you get care quickly if a problem appears.

notes_for_reviewer: Hip precautions differ by surgical approach (posterior vs anterior) and by surgeon. The page tells readers to follow their own surgeon's list and does not state a fixed duration. One fetch suggested OrthoInfo mentions about six weeks of precautions, but I could not confirm the exact wording, so I left it out.

Sources on structured hip rehab are thinner than for knee replacement. The Konnyu systematic review found low strength evidence that different programs give similar outcomes. The page uses it only to support following the surgeon's protocol. Its PMC page says 2022 (epub), and the issue citation is 2023, volume 102, page 11.

The intro attributes exercise guidance to AAOS. The specific methods (hip abductor strengthening, gait and balance training) are standard practice but are not tied to a single cited trial. Please confirm you are comfortable with them.
The 'more than 450,000 per year' figure comes from the AAOS OrthoInfo page as fetched. Recheck it if the page is updated.
Z47.1 needs a Z96.64x code to identify the hip. Billing staff should confirm the coding.
